Recap
• Americans are set to head to the polls today for the midterm elections to decide which political party controls Congress.
• The outcome will shape how much power Donald Trump has for the rest of his term.
• More than 50 million Americans have already voted, but many more ballots will be cast today.
• The US has conducted strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz on the eve of the country's midterm elections.
• We can expect to see the results rolling in from the morning of Wednesday, November 4, in Australia.
Stay with us as we bring you the latest updates.

What will Democrats do if the blue wave arrives in the House?
If Democrats win a House majority as the polls predict, the dynamics in Congress will completely change.
The party will have control over which bills get to the floor and will be able to stop Republicans from shepherding Donald Trump's agenda through Congress.

But they won't be able to pass much legislation on their own, because of barriers in the Senate (where most bills require 60 of 100 senators to even make it to a vote) and in the White House (where Donald Trump has veto powers).

Rather than legislation, Democrats' big focus is likely to be investigations. A House majority comes with significant powers to launch congressional probes, and Democrats are planning a flood of them.
Party leaders have indicated they want to investigate the ways Trump, his family and his corporate allies may have profited from his presidency.
Democrat Robert Garcia recently told The Atlantic he was maintaining a whiteboard with a "running list of the most corrupt things that the Trump family has done".
"There's a lot of ideas and possible investigations on there," he said.

The White House has been calling these plans "an extension of a decade-long witch hunt against President Trump". Trump has even floated the idea of giving pre-emptive pardons to his staff and allies like Elon Musk.
Some Democrats also want to use a House majority to impeach Trump — something they've done twice before. But many are reluctant to go down this path.

There looks to be more support in the party to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. A group of House Democrats filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April, relating to the Iran war and his running of the Defense Department, among other things.
"I think it's terrible," Trump said when asked about the possible impeachment push last week.
"All they do is talk about impeaching everybody."
▶️ Are the midterms headed for a Democratic 'bluenami'?
The Republican Party is tipped to lose seats in the midterms, but just how big will the blue wave be?
While Donald Trump is not on the ballot, his performance these past two years will impact how people vote, the ABC's chief elections analyst, Casey Briggs, explains.
Data on past elections shows that the party that holds the presidency nearly always goes backwards in the midterms.
Going back all the way to 1934, the president's party has lost an average of 27 seats.
This year, the Democrats will take back control of the House if they gain just three — and at the same time, Trump's net approval ratings have reached a new low.
Is all of Congress up for election?
Not quite.
All 435 seats in the House will be up for election, but only one-third of the Senate.
That's because while House members serve two-year terms, senators serve six-year staggered terms.
Thousands of observers expected at polls
Democrats and outside watchdogs are planning a massive presence at the polls, driven by concerns that President Donald Trump will leverage federal government resources to interfere with the results.

The election protection effort on the left is expected to deploy tens of thousands of monitors, who will be met at the polls by the largest-ever monitoring program by the Justice Department, and still more observers from Republican-aligned groups.
The effort among Democratic and non-profit groups includes training volunteers to stand watch outside polling places and report activities they consider concerning.

The Democratic National Committee's Association of State Democratic Committees created a first-of-its-kind cybersecurity unit staffed by former CIA and FBI officials to monitor and report online misinformation, including artificial intelligence deepfakes, said vice chair Jane Kleeb.

"We've never done this before," Kleeb said."We've never had to deal with the president of the United States saying that he may seize ballots, put ICE agents outside polling locations and other kinds of very clear direct threats to the voting process."
"We've never done this before," Kleeb said.

"We've never had to deal with the president of the United States saying that he may seize ballots, put ICE agents outside polling locations and other kinds of very clear direct threats to the voting process."
On Capitol Hill, Democratic leaders have assembled a legal team that rivals that of any presidential campaign.

While Trump continues to make baseless allegations of cheating in the election, administration and military officials have said they have no plans to deploy immigration agents or troops to polling sites.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis blamed "radical Democrats" for creating fears about election security by refusing to enact voter ID requirements and other Republican-backed measures.
"President Trump has done more than any other president to ensure we have free and fair elections," Bis said.
Reporting with AP
Polling is dire for Republicans, but can it be believed?
Polling predicts a crushing victory for Democrats in the House of Representatives, where they need to gain four seats.
There is even the possibility of Republicans losing their majority in the Senate.
Historically at midterm elections, control of the House can flip.
But a path to the Senate for Democrats is quite a turnaround for the party that started out having to "pitch a perfect game", as Jessica Taylor from the Cook Political Report puts it.
Trump's decision to launch a war on Iran has been pivotal in his sliding popularity.

"Typically, the president's party loses seats and certainly President Trump's approval ratings were not great before March, but pursuing an unpopular war that drove prices, especially on gasoline and diesel, further up has only put his party in more peril," Taylor said.

The latest on Iran-US negotiations
The war in Iran has become a major electoral issue, particularly as it exacerbates fuel prices and economic worries.
In the latest on Iran-US negotiations, a senior Iranian official has told Reuters a deal to end the war is still out of reach.
They reportedly said Tehran would not accept Washington's "excessive demands".
Meanwhile, Iran's parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, says the ball is now in America's court to "prevent war".

"The countries of the region should know that, just as the Islamic Republic of Iran stands ready for battle with its finger on the trigger, it has also given the American side a powerful and rational response," he said in a televised speech.
According to Pew Research Centre, 65% of Americans disapprove of Donald Trump's handling of US military action against Iran, compared with 33% who approve.
How many people have early voted?
More than 50 million Americans have already voted, with the turnout on pace to eclipse that of the last midterm elections two years ago.
And many more ballots will be cast today, local time.
In contrast to Trump's continued rhetoric about election cheating, voting so far has unfolded with relatively few problems.
But government watchdog groups worry that Trump and his loyalists could interfere with the voting process on election day.

Voting rights groups, Democrats and the Justice Department have been exchanging a flurry of legal filings over alleged non-citizen voters, federal election monitors and federal intimidation of election officials.
The findings reveal how Trump's attempts to expand federal control over state-run elections are resulting in court battles that could extend past election day into ballot counting.
Fearing a worst-case scenario, Democrats and nonpartisan watchdogs have trained tens of thousands of volunteers to monitor polling places.
Reporting with AP
Can Trump veto any bill passed by Congress?

I saw a clip recently of Trump referring to himself as 'Mr Veto' if Republicans lose significantly enough that Democrats are able to pass legislation. How strong is the president's veto power, and can he just say 'no' to anything he doesn't like?- Ry

I saw a clip recently of Trump referring to himself as 'Mr Veto' if Republicans lose significantly enough that Democrats are able to pass legislation. How strong is the president's veto power, and can he just say 'no' to anything he doesn't like?
- Ry
The short answer is: yes.
The president has the power to veto any bill passed by Congress, and that can only be overridden by a two-thirds majority in both chambers of Congress. It's safe to say that's not going to happen.
If Democrats win either chamber in Congress, there's a good chance it will lead to legislative gridlock (even more than is currently the case).
Key Event
Why are only some of the Senate seats up for election?
Why are only some of the senate seats up for election at the moment and not all of them?- Louise
Why are only some of the senate seats up for election at the moment and not all of them?
- Louise
Hi Louise — Senators serve six-year terms, and every two years one-third are up for election.
It's a bit like the Australian Senate, where members serve six-year terms, with half facing voters every federal election.
America's founding fathers wanted the Senate to be a more stable body, allowing members to take longer-term views on issues and be less affected by the whims of public opinion.

At the time the Constitution was being drafted, they considered longer or even lifetime terms. Six years was seen as a compromise between giving senators stability and keeping them accountable to voters.
Impeachment is largely a political act
One of the latest blog posts says that the Democrats could start a pathway to impeach Trump, what is alleged to have happened?- anonymous
One of the latest blog posts says that the Democrats could start a pathway to impeach Trump, what is alleged to have happened?
- anonymous
Given there's buckley's chance of President Donald Trump being convicted by the Senate, impeachment is largely a political act.
Democrats may have the numbers to pass articles of impeachment, but they would need to have a reason to as well.
You would think that Democrats would want to have an issue that would be seen as worthy of impeachment by the American public. The risk is that Democrats are seen as overplaying their hand.
Of course, people will disagree on exactly what the threshold is for "high crimes and misdemeanours".
Do results get released before polling booths close?
Do results start getting released before other polling booths are closed?- Bec
Do results start getting released before other polling booths are closed?
- Bec
In most states that straddle time zones, yes, we'll start to see figures in parts of the state while we wait for the rest of the state to close.
But we won't see any race calls for seats if parts of that seat are still voting.
How do the midterms work?
Hi! I don’t understand how the midterms really work. Are they similar to Australia’s state/suburb elections or just a poll on who’s voting for who at the moment? Thank you!- Lulu
Hi! I don’t understand how the midterms really work. Are they similar to Australia’s state/suburb elections or just a poll on who’s voting for who at the moment? Thank you!
- Lulu

The midterms are effectively parliamentary elections, with control of the legislative branch up for grabs. The presidency isn't on the ballot this year, but the parliament can be a thorn in the president's side, so the result is important.
Australia's Westminster political system is quite different to America, with the executive branch (the prime minister and government) being chosen by the legislative branch (the parliament).
At the same time, however, there are lots of local races, like council members, being elected.
Two years ago we made an entire program about how Americans vote for seemingly anything and everything.
📹: Here's our episode of America, Are You OK? on all the local races on the ballot in US elections.

What are the Senate and House races to watch?

Hi Casey! Thanks for sharing election day with us. Hope someone at the ABC finds a big digital map for you very soon... What are the House and Senate races you’ll have your eye on to get an early feel for how the night might unfold?- Nick

Hi Casey! Thanks for sharing election day with us. Hope someone at the ABC finds a big digital map for you very soon... What are the House and Senate races you’ll have your eye on to get an early feel for how the night might unfold?
- Nick

In the Senate, I'm watching North Carolina early in the day. Democrats are running former governor Roy Cooper, and if they're not winning in this state, that's a bad sign for their chances of flipping power there.
I'm also interested in knowing just how competitive South Carolina is. That's a state that has emerged as an interesting contest only in recent weeks, and it would be remarkable if it flipped.
After midday AEDT, we'll see votes in four key states: Texas, Michigan, Maine and Kansas.
Those states should give us a good idea of which way the winds are blowing, even if it takes a long time to call the races.
In the House, the list of races to watch is much longer, but here are a few to keep an eye on early in the day.
Take a look at Kentucky's 6th district. Trump won this district by 15 percentage points two years ago, but polling suggests a close race there.

In Florida, we're looking at a string of districts to see how much of an impact the out-of-cycle redistricting done by state Republicans has affected the makeup of Congress there. The Sunshine State might also give us some clues about whether Hispanic voters are swinging back towards Democrats after helping give Donald Trump a boost two years ago.

In North Carolina, I'm also keeping an eye on the 11th district, which Democrats are hopeful of picking up, and the 1st district in the north-east of the state. That's a seat that Republicans redistricted with the intention of improving their chances of victory, but incumbent Don Davis seems to have a good chance of overcoming that disadvantage.
Will Donald Trump be impeached a third time?
How much of a swing to the Democrats would put a successful impeachment in play?- Ashley
How much of a swing to the Democrats would put a successful impeachment in play?
- Ashley
Democrats would be able to impeach Donald Trump if they had a majority in the House of Representatives.
The process usually begins with an investigation into alleged treason, bribery or other "high crimes and misdemeanors" conducted by a House of Representatives committee.
A simple majority in the House can then pass articles of impeachment.
But that doesn't mean Donald Trump is removed from office.

After a successful impeachment vote, the Senate holds a "trial" to review the evidence, and the president is only convicted (and removed from the presidency) if a two-thirds majority passes the Senate. Democrats won't win enough states to give them the power to do that.
Key Event
Could the Democrats win both houses?
Hey Casey, is there any chance that the Democrats win both houses?- Sunyal
Hey Casey, is there any chance that the Democrats win both houses?
- Sunyal
There is absolutely a chance of that happening. In fact, polls suggest it's the most likely outcome.
Of course, the polls could be wrong, and if there's a polling miss, that means Democrats have been overstated and control of the Senate could become a much tighter contest.
What does a 'registered voter' mean?
Please explain the concept of a “registered Republican (or Democrat or independent) voter”. Is there an Australian equivalent concept?- Paul
Please explain the concept of a “registered Republican (or Democrat or independent) voter”. Is there an Australian equivalent concept?
- Paul
In many states, voters can register themselves with electoral authorities as a Democrat, a Republican or as an independent.

This is partly to enable voters to participate in open party primaries, where Democrats and Republican candidates compete against each other for the right to run as their party's endorsed candidate at a general election.
Typically, only voters registered with a party can participate in that party's primary elections.

While you would expect most registered Democrats to vote for Democratic candidates at general elections, and registered Republicans would vote for Republican candidates, there's no requirement for that.
It's very different to the way parties organise their internal structures and decision-making processes in Australia.

In Australia, we have no such concept of registering with a political party as part of our electoral enrolment. Instead, people who want to participate in pre-selections and party processes become members of their political parties.

There are thousands of different elections on the ballot across the country, all being fought in different districts.
Americans are electing state governors, legislators, judges, railroad commissioners, mayors, geological hazard abatement officers, and the list goes on!
There are also ballot measures and referendums around the country on topics ranging from data centre planning rules to abortion rights to requiring the Star-Spangled Banner to be sung in schools.

In Australia, we're most focused on the battle for Congress. Senate seats are statewide elections, while members of the House of Representatives represent districts within states, much like parliamentarians in our House of Reps.

Nearly every election is "first past the post", where the candidate with the highest number of votes is the winner. The exceptions are Maine and Alaska, which use ranked-choice voting. Australians are very familiar with that system: we call it preferential voting.
Why aren't the easternmost states the first to close?
Hey Casey. Why is it that Kentucky and Indiana close first when they’re not on the east coast?- Meredith
Hey Casey. Why is it that Kentucky and Indiana close first when they’re not on the east coast?
- Meredith
Great question, Meredith! The short answer is because those states have picked earlier closing times for polling places than the others.
Polls close at 6pm local time in Kentucky and Indiana. In most states, polls close at 7pm or 8pm.

Elections aren't conducted on a single set of national rules in the US. Every state is free to set its own rules, including counting procedures, voter ID requirements and when the polls are allowed to open.
Will our coverage continue throughout the night?
Are you going to do an all-nighter?- Kate
Are you going to do an all-nighter?
- Kate
Hi Kate — yes, our coverage will continue throughout the night, but luckily for us in Australia, tomorrow's an all-dayer!
One-third of Senate seats are up for election this year
How many of the 65 Senate seats that are not up for election are GOP or DEM?- Drew
How many of the 65 Senate seats that are not up for election are GOP or DEM?
- Drew
Hi Drew — There are 31 Republican senators who are partway through their terms and aren't up for election this year, and 35 Democrats.
Polls are closing across the US all day

You’ve said that votes will start to come in when polling booths close, but will that happen at different times for each timezone? And what time will the first and last ones shut? Thanks so much for your help!- Noah

You’ve said that votes will start to come in when polling booths close, but will that happen at different times for each timezone? And what time will the first and last ones shut? Thanks so much for your help!
- Noah
Strap in Noah, because it'll be a long, long day of vote counting.
The first polls close at 10am AEDT, but we start with just two states, and very red ones at that: Kentucky and Indiana.
At 11am, states including Florida, Georgia and South Carolina will start to close, followed by the key states of North Carolina and Ohio at 11:30am.
Then there's a big batch of key states where counting will begin from midday: Maine, Michigan, Kansas and Texas.
Polls will continue to close as the sun sets across America, with the final polling place due to close its doors at 5pm AEDT.
Key Event
By mid-afternoon, we should have a decent idea of which way things are going
At what time in Australian time are we likely to have an indication of the result?- Matt
At what time in Australian time are we likely to have an indication of the result?
- Matt

Hey Matt! If the polls are accurate, it might be that Democrats are flipping enough seats to take control in the House of Representatives by mid-afternoon AEDT (although they won't be able to cross the majority line of 218 until polls close in California in the late afternoon).
Depending on how competitive the battleground races are in the Senate, it could take a little longer to have a clear idea of that one.
If Democrats aren't picking up a state like North Carolina fairly quickly, it could mean we're in for a longer count.
But of course, it always depends on how close the contest is.
In the US, politics is dividing families
If you want to get a sense of how divided Americans are over politics, a tailgate before a Penn State football game is a good place to go.
In the sprawling carpark outside the university's massive stadium, people from all over the swing state gather to drink watery beers, eat burgers off the grill and often spend hours talking politics.
That's where the divisions become patently evident.

Joanne, 68, voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election, and although she feels he's behaved "horribly" since getting back into the White House, she's voting for Republicans down the ballot in her district in Western Pennsylvania.

"I don't believe in oversized government. The Democrats will just keep spending and spending and spend us into a hole," she told the ABC."I'm not happy with Trump's behaviour, but I agree with his economic policies and the Republican ethos."
"I don't believe in oversized government. The Democrats will just keep spending and spending and spend us into a hole," she told the ABC.
"I'm not happy with Trump's behaviour, but I agree with his economic policies and the Republican ethos."
Standing next to Joanne is Tim, her son-in-law.

"A lot of people are voting Republican even though they don't like Trump and don't want to say they've been brainwashed, but they've been brainwashed, sorry," he told the ABC, awkwardly looking over to his wife's mother."Politics has been the cause of division in our family; my father and I will fight like cats and dogs supporting Trump, but they never put forward any facts."

"A lot of people are voting Republican even though they don't like Trump and don't want to say they've been brainwashed, but they've been brainwashed, sorry," he told the ABC, awkwardly looking over to his wife's mother.
"Politics has been the cause of division in our family; my father and I will fight like cats and dogs supporting Trump, but they never put forward any facts."
Tim and Joanne hug and seem friendly, but rifts within American families have become increasingly common in a polarised America.
'One of the most tone-deaf presidential speeches'

Donald Trump's final pitch to voters ahead of the midterms was "one of the most tone-deaf presidential speeches" former BBC correspondent Nick Bryant has seen in his 30 years of covering the midterms.

"Here was Donald Trump talking for 20 minutes about his vanity projects in Washington — bizarre. The reflecting pool, the ceremonial arch he wants to build in Washington, and promenade on the Potomac," Bryant told Patricia Karvelas on Afternoon Briefing.
"At a time when so many Americans are suffering a cost-of-living crisis, to be talking about these schemes, which speak of his opulence and decadence, it is so out of sync.
"Donald Trump is a very clever politician. You don't get to be elected president of the United States twice if you are not a smart politician, but this was a very dumb move."

While oil prices dropped today after news of renewed diplomatic efforts to end the Iran war, the months-long cost-of-living crisis is too "baked in" for that to make a difference at this point, Bryant says.
Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs and the war in Iran are decisions voters can pinpoint as reasons they are struggling with the cost of living, Bryant says.
"Here there seems to be a villain for so many voters, and it is Donald Trump."
El-Sayed fans stand by their man amid Democratic infighting
You've probably heard of an "October surprise", but Democrat Haley Stevens's last-minute shock endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers was definitely this election's "November surprise".
It's still unclear if it'll hurt or help Abdul El-Sayed's chances of winning the Michigan Senate seat, but his supporters here in Detroit have been brushing off the drama.
Outside one of El-Sayed's rallies, Michigan voter Ali Tariq said he wasn't surprised by Stevens's move.
"I've always kind of seen her as like a closet Republican," he said."It's obvious that there's control over her and she's getting funding from certain groups and stuff, so it's not shocking."
"I've always kind of seen her as like a closet Republican," he said.
"It's obvious that there's control over her and she's getting funding from certain groups and stuff, so it's not shocking."
He's alluding to the fact Stevens got a huge funding injection for her campaign from AIPAC (a pro-Israel lobby group) during the primary against El-Sayed, which she narrowly lost in August.
The feud between her and El-Sayed erupted over his criticisms of Israel and US support for the country.

Roseanne Simons, who was wearing a "Jews for Abdul" badge, said while some within her community also disagreed with his positions on Israel, there was too much momentum behind him for the Stevens saga to derail his campaign.
"I support Abdul's stance on aid to Israel. I am a proud Jew. I do not support the Netanyahu government and what Israel is doing and what this country is complicit in helping Israel do."

This feud has also exposed a wider rift within the Democratic Party over its policies on Israel, which will no doubt continue to be a major issue beyond the midterms and into the 2028 presidential race (yes, we're already thinking about the next election before this one is even over).
Key Event
Democrats favoured to win control of both chambers
The Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.
Months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Wednesday.

According to the latest forecasts from Fifty Plus One, which aggregates the results of public opinion polls, the Democrats have a 99% chance of winning the House and an 80% chance of gaining control of the Senate.
But are the polls accurate?
There are plenty of examples from recent US history when public opinion polls were off the mark, particularly while Donald Trump has been in power.
There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day. Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race.
And sometimes undecided voters, who still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.
So it's worth keeping in mind there will always be some level of uncertainty that go with these forecasts.
Supreme Court rules against ignoring Californian ballots
In case you missed it, earlier today the US Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump's attempt to force California to sideline potentially thousands of ballots.
The federal government claims that these ballots may have been cast by non-citizens, flagging around 20,000 people on the largely Democratic state's voter rolls.
The court's swift rejection capped a string of losses for the president's effort to intervene in the election before the counting of ballots.
The court did not detail its reasoning in the California ballot case, as is common in emergency decisions.
"The Court rejected Trump's emergency request without even asking the other side to respond," California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, posted on X.
"Democracy won."
Non-citizen voting is illegal, and all available evidence shows that it is exceedingly rare.

But Trump, who falsely asserts that his loss in the 2020 presidential election was due to fraud, has long accused states — which are responsible for administering elections — of facilitating non-citizen voting.
Reporting with AP
Key Event
Do the midterms affect Trump?
Yes.
Trump may not be up for election right now, but the outcome of the midterms will shape how much power he has for the rest of his term.
Congress is responsible for making federal laws, controlling the budget and keeping the president in check.
And while Republicans currently control both chambers, they're at risk of losing them both.
Residents in battleground Michigan feel cost-of-living pain on election eve
I'm in Detroit, Michigan, the home of America's car manufacturing industry, nicknamed the "Motor City".
It's a sprawling network of highways and overpasses, so owning a car here is a necessity.
That means the soaring cost of fuel prices has hit Detroit residents particularly hard.
Some petrol stations we've passed have prices pushing $US5 a gallon (that's about $1.90 a litre).
That may sound on the cheaper side to Australians, and there are several reasons for that.
Australia's fuel excise is more than double the average total US fuel tax per litre. The US also produces a lot of its own fuel, while Australia imports it.
It's also relative; the median household income in Detroit is roughly half the national US average, so people are especially feeling the financial squeeze.
Michigan is home to a critical Senate battle at the midterm elections, and the cost of living is a major issue for voters.
The race is considered close, and while polls show the Democrat's vote increasing in many parts of the US, the Republicans are rated a chance to flip this seat.
We visited an auto repair shop in the city's north-east to hear how car owners were faring on the eve of the midterm elections.
Our visit coincided with new reporting from the Financial Times that petrol prices across the US are set to hit a record high of any administration one day before the midterms.

"It's astronomical," Ericka Hampton said, a tattoo artist who dropped in with her mum to get her car serviced."It's actually more expensive here than it even is in Texas. So it's crazy how we're the Motor City, but we're like getting slammed the hardest. It's crazy."
"It's astronomical," Ericka Hampton said, a tattoo artist who dropped in with her mum to get her car serviced.
"It's actually more expensive here than it even is in Texas. So it's crazy how we're the Motor City, but we're like getting slammed the hardest. It's crazy."
But it's not just the cost of filling up. Prices have crept up across the board, largely driven by inflation linked to the protracted war in Iran.
On top of that, Michigan is a border state, with Canada just a 15-minute drive from Detroit.
That means the effects of Donald Trump's expensive trade war and tariff policies have been particularly acute here.

"Everything's going up, and it's not going up month to month, it's going sometimes up day to day," Jay Salaytah said, owner of Jay's Auto Repairs shop."I can give a customer a price at four in the afternoon, they call me at 8am the next morning to authorise a repair, I go to order the parts, and all of a sudden the cost of these parts jumped up $30, $40."

Netanyahu is pushing for more Iran strikes: AP sources

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for another wave of strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections, the AP reports, citing two regional officials in the Middle East and a third person familiar with the matter.

The two officials said diplomatic efforts had made progress and mediators were trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the US lifting its blockade on Iran's ports.
The officials spoke to the AP on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American officials and one Israeli official.
Netanyahu pressed for strikes during a call over the weekend with Donald Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on the call.
The Israeli government did not immediately comment.
The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trump's discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call.
Reporting with AP
In close races, some Republicans are distancing themselves from Trump
Distancing yourself from Donald Trump was once a career-ending move for a Republican.
Now, an analyst says it has become a political necessity for many GOP candidates.

While Trump has been eager to frame the midterms as a referendum on a second term, Republican candidates in tight races across the country are working to assure voters that their orders will not come from the White House.
Hans Noel, a political scientist at Georgetown University, said a Trump endorsement was no longer the asset it once was.
"I think one of the things that Republican candidates have found is that Trump is incredibly unpopular, historically unpopular," Noel said.
"And with that, they figure his coat-tails aren't going to be really useful."
The shift is visible in critical battlegrounds. In close races, candidates such as senator Susan Collins of Maine are striving to project independence.
"Susan Collins has basically been saying, 'I'm not a Donald Trump stooge,'" Noel said.
Key Event
When will we know the result?
Officials will start counting votes once the polls close in their state — and results will start being known within a few hours.
Most of the public's votes should be counted on election night in the US.
But because each state has different rules about how ballots are counted and reported, it could take longer in some jurisdictions.
Even if a state counts quickly, we might not see races officially called for days if the margins are close.
Trump's last speech before voting begins
Trump says his Republican Party is facing an uphill battle at the midterm elections this week, amid polling that suggests he could lose control of Congress.
In his final major campaign event before the elections, Trump was quick to highlight the historical trend that the sitting president's party "doesn't win the midterms".
"But we gave this a very strong shot," he said during a speech in Washington DC on Monday afternoon, local time.
He later described the votes that would take place on Tuesday, local time, as "the most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime".
"We have to keep our Congress strong and free," he said.
Trump also said the Democratic Party had nominated "the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history".

▶️ Texans share who they're voting for in the midterms

The Senate race in long-term red state Texas is expected to be a close one between Democrat candidate James Talarico, who is holding a slight lead in most polls since September, and Republican candidate Ken Paxton.
Much like in the polling, Texan voters interviewed by the ABC at a San Antonio breakfast taco shop had mixed views on who they're casting their votes for.
"I go all Republican. I'm not for the Democrats. I don't think they do a good job," one woman said, adding that she would be casting her vote for Paxton and "all the Republicans".
"James Talarico seems to do a lot more for the people. He's Christian-based," another patron said.
"And so just the stuff that he's talked about, I feel a lot better about voting for him than anybody else."

What are the Senate races to watch?
Democrats need to flip at least four seats in the US Senate to gain control of the chamber.
A takeover looked unlikely at the start of this year, but Democrats are now competitive in several states Trump won comfortably in 2024.
The party is hoping to capture Republican-held seats in Alaska, Kansas, Maine, Nebraska, Ohio and Texas, to name a few. Meanwhile, the GOP is trying to flip Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire.
Trump 'going to states he shouldn't need to'
Tracking the states Donald Trump has been campaigning in provides clues as to where his Republican Party believes its biggest concerns are.
The president has made 28 trips to various states to campaign since October 1.
His itinerary is revealing. Many analysts believe the Democrats will seize control of the House in these midterm elections, but polls suggest the Senate contests are more competitive.
This map shows where Trump has been over the past few weeks, and who controls the Senate seats up for grabs in the states he has visited.
In some states that Trump used to be able to count on for solid support, polls suggest some of the Senate contests are now a toss-up, or at least closer than the Republicans would like.
For example, the president has been to Texas multiple times to stump for GOP Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
The Democrats have not won a Senate seat in the state for 33 years, but many polls suggest the party has a narrow lead in the contest.
Kansas is a really interesting case. The state has not elected a Democratic senator for almost a century, but the Senate race there is on a knife edge, according to multiple predictions.

"He's visiting red states that he won by double figures only two years ago, so that's an indication of the concern that's gripping the White House at this point," James D Boys, a long-time political academic and the author of multiple books on US presidents, told the ABC.

So what's up for grabs?
All 435 seats in the House and 35 of the seats in the Senate.
Donald Trump's Republican Party currently controls both chambers of Congress.
The Democrats are hoping to flip enough seats to win a majority. If they win control of at least one chamber, they will gain power to bring their own laws to the floor.

What is a midterm election?
Americans vote on who their next president is every four years.
But they have the chance to decide which political party controls Congress (the US House of Representatives and the Senate) more often.
When a president is being voted in, seats in both chambers are up for election as well.
And then halfway through the president's term, voters can head back to the polls to shake Congress up again.
This is known as the midterm election.
